items.text:
Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say
An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.
Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed.
The new approach, which combines BMI with other body measurements and organ function tests, suggests BMI alone misses obesity in 5-9% of adults, while wrongly diagnosing the condition in as many as 3%.
“This misclassification can account for tens of millions of people, so the inaccuracy of BMI is a big problem at scale and also for individuals,” said Francisco Rubino, a professor of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London.
BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. About 1.6 billion people worldwide are classified as overweight, meaning their BMI falls between 25 and 29.9, and nearly a billion with a BMI of 30 or more are considered obese. Two-thirds of adults in the UK and more than 70% of adults in the US are overweight or obese based on BMI alone.
Rubino and his colleagues drew on health records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain to test a diagnostic approach for obesity that he and other world experts proposed last year in a Lancet Commission report . They used the records to track people’s health for up to 15 years.
Under the new definition, someone with a BMI over 40 is considered obese, but doctors check people with a lower BMI for excess body fat by looking at their waist measurement.
A BMI of 30-plus with a raised waist measurement or waist-to-height ratio counts as obese, as does a BMI from 25 to 29.9 if waist measurement and waist-to-height ratio are high. In most countries, a raised waist measurement means more than 102cm (40in) for men and 88cm for women, while thresholds for a high waist-to-height ratio are about 0.57.
In a second step of the diagnosis, doctors distinguish between clinical obesity, meaning an active disease where excess body fat is already impairing organ function, and pre-clinical obesity, where the extra fat is a health risk but has yet to cause problems.

items.text:
“It was like looking for a needle in a haystack.”
That’s how Professor Daniel Mège described the discovery of trace volcanic gases on Mars that could be key to finding life on the Red Planet.
The discovery centers around hydrogen chloride gas seeping out through volcanic rifts—something of a “smoking gun” that suggests Mars is not geologically dead, but merely sleeping.
These gases hint at magma, which, when coming into contact with groundwater can produce warm habitable niches for organisms beneath the Red Planet’s surface.
“If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface,” one of the scientists behind the discovery hypothesized.
Mars is studded with the largest volcanoes in the solar system, and fresh fissures on the surface of one of the largest, called Alba Mons, hint at volcanically active spots under the surface.
Detected by a European Space Agency (ESA) orbiter, an international research team believes that the release of hydrogen chloride from these fissures comes from hot magma beneath the surface.
The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first reported hydrogen chloride gas in the Martian atmosphere in 2021. The gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, leading researchers to wonder whether the same was happening on Mars.
Evidence for active volcanism on Mars has always been extremely elusive, yet enough has been identified in the form of geologically-recent lava flows and “marsquakes” over the last 50 years, so as never to rule it out.
Now again, researchers noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride where they shouldn’t have been, and during an odd season in the northern hemisphere of Mars.
Study co-leader Professor Daniel Mège, from the Space Research Center of the Polish Academy of Sciences, said the gas varies seasonally on Mars, reaching its maximum in the northern winter, then mostly disappearing in the summer.
But there was one exception to the pattern, always in the same season and at the same place: above volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer.
A close look at the Alba Mons region using TGO’s infrared spectroscopy instrument showed fresh and narrow fissures, in some cases hundreds of yards in length, associated with color changes on the surface.

Kasparov secured the world crown in Moscow by a score of 13–11 making him the youngest champion in history at just 22 years of age, and began a reign of dominance that ranks him among the best in history. The Kasparov-Karpov rivalry was to play out in four matches across four different world championships from 1984 to 1990, with Kasparov claiming the world title by narrow margins of 12½–11½ in 1986, 12–12 in 1987, and 12½–11½ in 1990.
The win in Moscow set Kasparov on course to eventually hold the record for the longest time as the No. 1 rated player in the world—from 1984 to 2005. At the time of his retirement in 2005, he was still ranked No. 1 in the world, with a rating of 2812.
Kasparov holds the record for most consecutive professional tournament victories, placing first or equal first in fifteen individual tournaments from 1981 to 1990.

Lamarr is one of the most remarkable women of the 20th century, and has been described as one of the greatest actresses of all time. Alongside George Antheil, a musical composer, Lamarr developed a radio-wave guidance system that was hoped to allow Allied torpedoes to break through the Nazi’s radar jamming systems, but led to the invention of Wi-Fi and Bluetooth instead.
Hedy Lamarr had a successful film and theater career as an actress in Austria, including for an award-ridden portrayal of Empress Elisabeth of Austria in Sissy (1933). items.desc: A viral moment from a doorbell camera that reached millions of people has now raised more than $76,000 to support a woman who spends her days caring for others. When Suzanna Metcalf arrived at Pastor Neal Seiwert’s home in Castle Rock, Colorado last year, she apologized as she had mixed up their pizza order, and […] The post A Viral Video Led Strangers to Raise $76,000 for a Full-Time Caregiver ap
items.text:
A viral moment from a doorbell camera that reached millions of people has now raised more than $76,000 to support a woman who spends her days caring for others.
When Suzanna Metcalf arrived at Pastor Neal Seiwert’s home in Castle Rock, Colorado last year, she apologized as she had mixed up their pizza order, and would have to return with the correct order. She blamed “getting old,” but the struggle on her face was clear.
Metcalf works delivery shifts while serving as the full-time caregiver for her 82-year-old mother, managing daily care, medical needs and household expenses.
Instead of frustration, Seiwert, his wife Hailee, and their three young daughters stepped outside, placed their hands on her shoulders, and prayed for her. The short clip, captured by a doorbell camera, showed Metcalf visibly moved by the unexpected kindness after a long day of work.
The video, posted by Seiwert, quickly went viral, with hundreds of commenters, who almost all had the same question: How can we help?
The Seiwerts found Metcalf, and with her permission, started a GoFundMe, which describes Suzanna as a woman who has spent years putting others first.
What began as a modest effort quickly grew. More than 2,600 donors have contributed over the last year, raising over $76,000 — far exceeding the initial $10,000 goal— to give Suzanna some financial breathing room as she continues caring for her mom.
Seiwert told the New York Post he wanted Metcalf to feel both his family’s support and a broader sense of being valued. “So many people are commenting on how it brought them to tears. There are many people who simply just need love,” he said.
A viral moment doesn’t change the demands of caregiving and delivery work. But it has shown, in concrete form, that one small pause for kindness can open the door for real help.

items.title: 71 Awful Teachers Who Went Above And Beyond To Make Students Miserable
items.desc: Every school year, parents stock up on uniforms, school shoes, textbooks and stationery to give their children the best chance of success. But none of these essentials count for much when the person in charge of the classroom is less Miss Honey and more Miss Trunchbull. Most teachers deserve far more credit than they get, but these students weren’t so lucky.
items.text:
One of the most memorable teachers from my school days was a tall woman with flaming red hair and eyes that felt like they could see straight through to your soul. Legend had it she’d spend detention sitting at the front of the classroom having her long red nails filed and painted while the students wrote lines. There was even a rumor that a girl once wet herself in her class, though no one could say for sure whether it was out of fear or because she simply wasn’t allowed to leave.
I remember the day I found out I’d be in her class, and all the sobbing that followed. But funnily enough, I now look back on her fondly. She was firm, sure, but she was fair, and she had a way of making you want to rise to the occasion. I learned a lot in that classroom , and when she eventually left, I genuinely missed her.
I can’t say the same for a couple of the teachers I had later on. They had far less colorful reputations (and no long red nails), but they stand out in my memory for all the wrong reasons, and my grades reflected it. And I’m sure plenty of people can relate. Most of us have a story or two about a teacher who failed us in some way—and not necessarily academically.
So why do these teachers stay with us long after we’ve forgotten almost everything else about school? Researchers have actually looked into it. In a 2022 study , 157 adults were asked to describe up to three of their most significant experiences with teachers during childhood and adolescence.
Never miss a story that brings joy to the world. Add us on Google
Of the 423 experiences participants described, roughly a quarter involved a teacher being unjust or degrading. And those memories appeared to have a lasting association with well-being. Participants whose most significant experience fell into this category tended to have lower self-esteem as adults, suggesting that a negative experience with a teacher can stay with someone long after they’ve left the classroom.
These kinds of experiences are also more common than you might expect. In a 2025 study involving 271 college students, 43% said they had been bullied by a teacher at least once during their school years . When the researchers asked them to describe what happened, 82% of the accounts met their criteria for mistreatment. And much like the earlier research, those who had been through it were more likely to struggle with self-esteem and motivation later on.

items.title: Print commissioned by Nasa uncovered for exhibition
items.desc: The Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition tells the story of the British International Print Biennale.
items.text:
Komtek I (left) was created in 1968 from an early computer image
A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.
Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.
The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.
The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.
While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.
"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.
"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.
In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.
John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.
Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.
He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.
Cartwright Hall is home to one of Andy Warhol's famous Marilyn prints
Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.
It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.
Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.
Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.

items.title: Toby Jones stars in film about UK Mars mission
items.desc: Mackenzie Crook directs the story of the British professor whose probe lost contact upon touchdown.
items.text:
The film has been funded by BBC Film, BFI, Sky, Screen Yorkshire and CML Entertainment Finance
Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".
Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.
The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.
Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."
Pillinger died believing that Beagle 2 had not safely landed on Mars
Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.
Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.
His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.
The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.
Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.
Mars Express is the first feature-length film to be directed by actor Mackenzie Crook
The director added: "Joe Bone's beautiful script has made it easy to attract some of the best names in the business to join our brilliantly creative team and I'm thrilled to be working once again with my friend Toby Jones."
Crook, known for his roles in The Office and Pirates of the Caribbean, previously worked with Jones on Detectorists , the BBC's Bafta-winning comedy he wrote, directed and starred in.
He also starred in Small Prophets, a comedy which made its debut on BBC Two and the BBC iPlayer in February.
The film is expected to be released in 2027.

items.title: Scientists predict 2026 hottest year on record as climate talks begin
items.desc: Scientists are predictng this could be the hottest year on record as the COP31 climate summit opens.
items.text:
From Western Europe to Indonesia, countries have battled wildfires throughout 2026 following record heat from climate change and El Niño
The world is on course for its hottest year on record as the planet is hit with warming from climate change and El Niño, scientists have told BBC News.
The warning comes as world leaders and negotiators gather in Turkey on Monday for the opening of COP31, the latest UN climate summit.
Berkeley Earth, the independent US research group behind the forecast, said that even with two months of the year left it is 95% confident that 2026 will surpass the previous record set in 2024.
The impact of rising heat has been felt acutely in recent months by countries attending COP, with extensive wildfires across Europe and the sudden glacier collapse in Nepal which killed more than 1,000 people.
"We have had a run of record warm years," said Dr Robert Rohde, of Berkeley Earth. "That is what we expect as global warming progresses… glaciers collapsing, record-breaking heatwaves and droughts."
On Friday, the EU's Copernicus climate service , external confirmed that October was the hottest on record.
But Rohde warned this was just the start. "There is potential for much larger and much more dramatic changes down the line," he said.
The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
The UN's World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published its own report on Monday , external , and although more cautious than Berkeley, it has forecast that 2026 will be among the four warmest years on record.
It said that 2027 will provide no let-up, as an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year, pushing temperatures higher.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said it "gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts".
The findings underline the challenge facing negotiators gathering in the seaside Turkish city of Antalya for COP31.
At previous meetings the focus has been on reducing emissions - tackling the cause of climate change. But now an increasing number of nations are facing the reality of having to do that alongside adapting to new weather extremes as the planet warms.

items.title: The Maya Loved Using Mercury-Rich Red Paint to Decorate Pottery, Temple Walls and Even Burials. They May Have Accidentally Poisoned Their Own Water and Food Supply in the Process
items.desc: Testing of ancient sediment from two lakes in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula has revealed "crazy" high concentrations of mercury, as one researcher puts it, confirming findings from other regions of the Mesoamerican civilization
items.text:
The Maya loved cinnabar , a bright red ore used to decorate pottery, burial sites, structures and more. But cinnabar is roughly 86 percent mercury , a highly toxic element that can harm humans, animals and ecosystems.
The Maya used so much of this prized pigment that they polluted some of their cities. Now, new research suggests the Maya’s cinnabar-derived mercury contamination was even more widespread than previously thought—and it could have contributed to the civilization’s downfall.
Testing of ancient sediment from two lakes in modern-day Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula has revealed high concentrations of mercury during ancient Maya occupation. The findings, published November 4 in the journal Science Advances , suggest mercury pollution took a toll on the lakes’ aquatic ecosystems, causing their populations of aquatic creatures to decline or collapse. If the Maya ate fish or drank water from the lakes, they could have been exposed to toxic concentrations of mercury for decades or even centuries.
In 2022, scientists reported finding high levels of mercury at several archaeological sites in the Maya’s southern highlands and south-central lowlands, attributing the contamination to the use of cinnabar. The new study, conducted by a different team of researchers, builds on that work, investigating mercury levels at bodies of water in the Maya’s northern lowlands.
Researchers stuck long, heavy, hollow cylinders deep into the lakebeds of two lakes near ancient Maya cities, Coba and Xcach (pronounced “scotch”). They pulled up thick columns of sediment that had preserved centuries of environmental history, layer by layer.
At one site, Lago Coba, the sediment revealed centuries of elevated mercury levels, lasting from around 40 C.E. to 300 C.E. That corresponds with the end of the late Preclassic Period and the beginning of the Classic Period , which is considered the golden age of Maya civilization.
At Cenote Xcach, mercury levels spiked three different times: First, from roughly 125 C.E. to 200 C.E., just before the Classic Period; again, from 330 to 350 C.E., in the middle of the Classic Period; and, finally, from 535 C.E. to 820 C.E., toward the end of the Classic Period.

Takumi Kama, “The First Appearance KAIJU,” 2026, Japan. Acrylic color. Cotton on wood panel. L162×W130.3×H3.5cm(F100). Courtesy of the artist and COMBINE / BAMI gallery
In Japanese pop culture, a kaiju is a mythical monster of great proportions. They have long been symbols of chaos and destruction, serving society as cathartic vehicles to dealing with difficult times and challenging situations. In media, they could symbolically manifest as World War II and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, or natural disasters that make humankind feel powerless in the face of nature. More than anything, though, kaiju represent the consequences of human actions—or inactions.
These fantastical creatures inspired Japanese artist Takumi Kama to tackle a more recent and universal topic. In his aptly titled KAIJU series, these towering beasts aren’t made of flesh and blood. Instead, their bodies are an accumulation of the things we consume and quickly discard, whether physical or digital. “In other words,” the artist says, “it exists like a mirror reflecting us—the very people who are looking at this work—and perhaps it could even be described as a self-portrait of us as human beings.”
These kaiju loom in dark alleys and the morning fog, for which they can be accidentally run into. Some feature imagery from the Edo period, as the artist wonders how these creatures would have looked in that time, while others are more contemporary, made up of pixels or pop culture, junk food, and plastic trinkets.
Kama recently presented his work at Art Taipei, where he was one of the most talked about creatives for his unique approach to modern culture and our increasingly digitalized lives. As such, COMBINE/BAMI Gallery , which represents the artist, will offer plenty of chances to check out the artist’s work from up close. From late December 2026 through early January 2027, the gallery will present many of Kama’s works in an annual exhibition centered on the theme of the Chinese zodiac, spotlighting the artist’s charming and playful style.
Next year, COMBINE/BAMI Gallery will open a dual exhibition featuring Kama and fellow Japanese painter Hisashi Matsumoto in March. Before that, his work will be exhibited at Osaka International Art 2027, taking place January 29-31, 2027 (VIP Preview on January 28, 2027).

items.text:
A 1763 map of Jamaica showing the island’s parishes, settlements, and geographical features. (Photo: Thomas Craskell, Henry Moore, James Simpson, and Daniel Fournier via Library of Congress , Public Domain )
Tracing your family tree can sometimes lead to unexpected discoveries, but for descendants of enslaved people, finding information about their ancestors can be especially difficult. Ancestry is hoping to make that process a little easier with the release of nearly 4 million records documenting enslaved individuals across 20 former British colonies. They span across the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Indian Ocean, and South Africa. They include places such as Jamaica, Barbados, the Bahamas, Trinidad, Mauritius, and South Africa.
Released on September 22, 2026, the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers collection includes around 300,000 digitized pages dating from 1813 to 1840. For the first time, the records have been fully indexed and made searchable online, giving descendants across the African diaspora a new way to explore their family histories.
“For descendants of enslaved individuals, family history research may often present a set of unique challenges to overcome, but what makes this collection so groundbreaking is its extraordinary level of detail,” says Nicka Sewell-Smith, professional genealogist and Senior Story Producer at Ancestry. “Featuring names, ages, and family connections, these registers give descendants across the diaspora a real opportunity to solve longstanding family mysteries and speak their ancestors’ names back into history.”
The proclamation of the abolition of slavery in Jamaica in Spanish Town on August 1, 1838. (Photo: Thomas Ashburton Picken via Wikimedia Commons , Public Domain )
Depending on the individual record, researchers may find names, ages, genders, family relationships, physical descriptions, births, deaths, and even information about a person’s African origins before enslavement. Details like these can be especially valuable for people trying to trace family histories that were disrupted by slavery.
The registers themselves have a much darker origin. Following Britain’s abolition of the transatlantic slave trade in 1807, the government required colonies to document enslaved populations in an effort to prevent illegal trafficking. These records were ultimately created as part of a system that treated human beings as property and kept track of enslaved populations before emancipation.

items.text:
A coat once placed over the shoulders of a young girl whose traditional Korean uniform had been slashed in a racial incident 30 years ago has now been returned to the ‘good Samaritan’ who offered it.
Norihisa Koyama was a Japanese high school student at the time of the notorious “hanbok slashing incidents” when he saw a girl whose clothes were torn.
“A female student was crouching down and crying. I knew something was seriously wrong.”
The teen then gave her his brand new winter coat, just bought for him by his parents, to the Korean school student whose hanbok jacket (the traditional national attire of Korea) had been intentionally sliced open in public with a knife or scissors.

items.text:
GNN Voices is a new series of first-person pieces from people worth listening to: practitioners, researchers, teachers, and neighbors sharing what they’ve learned and how they see things.
My dad’s name was Kiran. In Sanskrit, it means “a ray of light.”
I wrote my book, Making Sense of Purpose , in his memory. His name is in the subtitle.
My dad found a way to walk with people without carrying them; he found a way to guide them without giving them directions; he held space, he held hands, he held space for their wants, needs and expectations, and then he shined a light on what made them and mattered to them and what’s forward …
This week is Diwali, the festival of lights. This year, I want to make it a gift to everyone. A week to shine a light back on the year and move forward with purpose before we rush into the new one.
Wanting to avoid a doom scroll is hard. But giving people something to do instead maybe helps.
It happens more because of the environment we built than because of any flaw in us. We grab what fills us without considering whether it nourishes us.
A few minutes of reflection pays us back. Researchers at Harvard Business School found that new employees who spent the last 15 minutes of each training day writing and reflecting on what they’d learned performed 22.8% better on their final test.
Ten questions. Five days. One in the morning, one at night. A few minutes each. Write it down, or just reflect and take note. Either way counts.
We’re bad at knowing what will make us happy. We rarely get explicit about what made a good moment good. So we never ask people what made them happy; we ask what makes them smile as they reflect.
We are strengths to be harnessed. Not weaknesses to be fixed. And our values are who we are when the world is at its messiest. Kennon Sheldon and Andrew Elliot found that when our goals come from our values, we put in more sustained effort and are more likely to reach them.
Not every plateau needs to be broken. Self-forgiveness is the single most powerful action, wholly within your control, that allows you to empty your backpack. When we forgive ourselves, the likelihood going forward is that we’ll be faster to break free than if we carry the guilt forward. And big wins are made by small steps.
As David McRaney puts it, Anxiety = Fear + Uncertainty. Sorting what we can control, what we can influence and what is outside our control makes uncertainty feel less overwhelming. And compassion is about caring, not carrying.

During World War II, the medieval stained glass of Coventry Cathedral was dismantled and hidden in crates to survive air raids. Now, an ambitious cataloging project has digitized roughly 12,000 fragments, making them publicly accessible for the first time in decades.
On November 14, 1940, German bombers obliterated the cathedral, making it the only British cathedral destroyed during the Blitz . The glass survived, stashed in 30 wooden crates in the rectory cellars of a nearby village, remaining there until 1957. The red sandstone cathedral was eventually rebuilt and its old charred shell was preserved as a memorial to peace and reconciliation. But the windows were never reassembled.
As Coventry marks the 86th anniversary of the bombing, the World Monuments Fund (WMF) and cathedral curators have photographed and cataloged the fragile trove, launching a digital exhibition on the Bloomberg Connects app .
“Coventry Cathedral’s collection of medieval stained glass, which includes exquisitely executed examples of 15th-century painting, is of international importance,” Laura Atkinson , a stained-glass conservator who led the cataloging, says in a statement . “Yet it has received little scholarly study. The assemblage— Britain’s largest collection of loose medieval stained glass—dates largely to the 15th century. The fragments are attributed to John Thornton , one of medieval England’s master glaziers, famed for creating the Great East Window at York Minster.

A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.
And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.
As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.
America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

items.text:
Dormice have become much rarer in the UK as woodlands and hedgerows are lost
Dormouse numbers may be recovering in England and Wales after years of decline, offering a rare piece of good news for one of our best-loved mammals.
The animal has disappeared from much of the countryside with conservationists warning of a long-term collapse in its population.
However, new data suggests dormouse numbers increased between 2020-2025, a period that coincided with warmer springs and summers.
Scientists believe these conditions may help dormice survive, by boosting food supplies and reducing the time they spend asleep.
That gives the animals more opportunity to breed and build up fat reserves ahead of winter.
Even during spring and summer, when it's cold and wet, dormice can go into short periods of deep sleep
But conservationists caution that many questions remain unanswered, and say protecting the woodlands and hedgerows where dormice live remains essential to their long-term survival.
The only native species of dormice in the UK is the hazel dormouse. Once widespread across the country, they are now largely confined to southern England and parts of Wales. They have become much rarer as large areas of woodland are lost and so far native populations have disappeared from around 20 English counties.
The National Dormouse Monitoring Programme, led by the conservation charity People's Trust for Endangered Species (PTES), has been monitoring sites in England and Wales since 1998.
It found that since 2000, dormouse numbers have fallen by almost 60%, equivalent to an average annual decline of 3.5%.
More recently, however, there are signs that trend may be reversing. The data suggests the population increased by almost 10% between 2020 and 2025, although researchers stress there is considerable uncertainty around that estimate.
The apparent improvement coincides with a period of warmer, drier-than-average springs and summers.
Report co-author Ian White of PTES described the "upturn" as "welcome good news" which gives grounds for "cautious optimism".
But he added: "We mustn't lose sight of the bigger picture: populations remain almost 60% lower than they were in 2000."

I n his one-paragraph short story , On Exactitude in Science, Jorge Luis Borges imagines an empire in which the level of cartographical ambition is so high that a map is made on a one-to-one scale with the imperial territory. The quest for perfect accuracy doesn’t end well. But the earliest map-makers for Ordnance Survey, which this week marked the 225th anniversary of its first publication, might have empathised with the obsessive dedication.
The 1801 OS map of Kent was 10 years in the making, its military-led production inspired by fears of Napoleonic invasion. But as Rachel Hewitt points out in Map of a Nation , her stirring account of the Ordnance Survey’s early years, its genesis also lay in an Enlightenment-based enthusiasm for comprehending and accurately representing reality. During the course of the 19th century, the entirety of the British isles was meticulously mapped through fog, rain, wind and sun, in what was described as “a wild and arduous exercise”. The surveyors, armed with theodolites, measuring chains and notebooks, saw themselves as footsoldiers serving in the ranks of Reason as they brought intellectual order to the landscape.

Doctors have made a potentially significant breakthrough in the hunt for a treatment for stiff person syndrome, the autoimmune condition that affects the singer Céline Dion .
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disease that attacks the central nervous system and can cause devastating rigidity throughout the body and painful muscle spasms. Despite decades of research, there is no cure.
Now a team of neurologists in the US trialling a novel form of immunotherapy have reported “exciting” and “very encouraging” results: the treatment has prompted dramatic improvements in people living with SPS.
Patients who previously needed help with basic daily tasks and struggled to walk have regained their ability to take part in everyday life, with some even returning to work and resuming hobbies, according to doctors at the Mayo Clinic.
The novel treatment, CAR-T cell therapy, is already used to treat cancer, and reprogrammes a patient’s immune cells to help fight disease. During the study, SPS patients’ own T cells, a type of immune cell, were extracted and engineered to wipe out disease-causing cells.
Neurologists said the results, published in medical journal Jama Neurology, were particularly exciting because patients had been able to return to activities they feared they would never be able to return to.
Dr Anastasia Zekeridou, a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, said: “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients.
“With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function. These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time.”
Jonathan Walden, one of the patients in the trial, had reached the point where walking and basic daily tasks required help from his family. But after CAR-T, he has returned to work.
“I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.”

Down Under comedy has an innate “tall poppy syndrome.” It’s the social habit of cutting down or mocking anyone who boasts, stands out, or gets too successful.
The phrase comes from a garden where a few poppies grow taller than the rest, prompting the gardener to chop off the tallest heads so every flower stays level. In Australia, this mindset is a constant target for local humor and self-deprecating banter.
Venezuelan-Australian comedian Ivan Aristeguieta even mined laughs from the name itself, joking that he initially misheard it as “tall puppy syndrome."
Researchers at the University of Melbourne found that the term tall poppy syndrome gained popularity across Australia and New Zealand in the 1980s, reflecting cultural values of equality and humility.
In a New Zealand study of prominent entrepreneurs, nearly all reported encountering it firsthand. As one put it, “If you do achieve something and stick your head up a bit further, people will try to chop you down to size.”
Australia’s unique sense of humor recently sparked an online conversation after a British expat asked Reddit if Aussie banter still belonged in the office. He said his newer co-workers seemed genuinely shocked by it. The post triggered nearly a thousand responses from locals and expats alike.
Many worried that traditional workplace banter is going extinct as “sensitive” employees label everyday ribbing as offensive. Others said that office culture is simply evolving and drawing a firm line between playful teasing and actual disrespect.
Experts believe Aussie humor can be weird and confusing, especially if you’re new to the culture.
“An Australian friend may greet you with an insult so creative that a stranger would assume a fight was about to begin. Instead, it is often a sign of affection. The closer the friendship, the less polite the conversation. It makes little sense. But it works. Beneath the teasing lies something important: Authenticity,” says Rick LeCouteur, a retired veterinarian and author .

Installation view, Yoshitomo Nara, David Zwirner, New York, November 5—December 12, 2026.
Japanese artist Yoshitomo Nara is bringing his instantly recognizable characters back to New York with a major exhibition at David Zwirner. Spanning two of the gallery’s Chelsea locations, the presentation features nearly 100 works, including new paintings, drawings, recent sculptures, and selections from earlier decades. It marks Nara’s first solo exhibition with David Zwirner and his first major solo presentation in New York in nearly a decade.
Best known for his oversized, wide-eyed figures, Nara has developed a visual language that balances playful imagery with a rebellious edge. His young-looking subjects often appear innocent at first glance, but their expressions suggest something more complicated. Some stare directly at the viewer with quiet defiance, while others carry an unmistakable sense of melancholy. Beneath their cartoonlike appearance, Nara’s characters confront ideas about childhood, vulnerability, resistance, and the realities of the world around them.
The exhibition also traces the development of Nara’s distinctive style. Earlier works from the late 1980s and 1990s appear alongside new pieces, offering a closer look at how his imagery has evolved. His latest paintings introduce muted colors and layered surfaces, while large-scale monochromatic drawings made with industrial paint sticks reveal the expressive energy of his drawing practice.
At the gallery’s 19th Street location, 13 monumental bronze sculptures transform the space. Coated in matte white, the oversized heads recall the snow-covered forests near Mount Hakkōda in northern Japan, where Nara grew up. Their imposing scale contrasts with their softly illuminated surfaces, creating an atmosphere of stillness. Together, the sculptures connect his familiar characters to the natural landscapes and childhood memories that continue to inform his work.
Yoshitomo Nara is on view at David Zwirner’s galleries at 533 West 19th Street and 537 West 20th Street in New York City from November 5 through December 12, 2026. Visit David Zwirner for additional information and exhibition details.

“He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail.” That’s how one rescuer in Kentucky described the moment he spotted 6-year-old Roman Heilman, a boy with autism missing for 3 days.
Jacob Mullins, a member of a local horse trailriding group, told the Lexington Herald Leader that he was only about a half-mile from Heilman’s home when he suddenly climbed out of a bush followed by a small dog, and and sang “Old McDonald.”
Heilman then grabbed onto the leg of the lead rescuer and didn’t want to let go.
He had been reported missing in the late afternoon on Sunday, November 1st, and the volunteers had been out since first light on Tuesday, looking around the wooded and mountainous area for hours, covering some 14 miles.

items.desc: More people are swapping animal products with vegan milks, yogurts and cheeses, so scientists wanted to investigate the potential public health effects. Their findings hint that consumers should look for items with extra nutrients added, called fortified foods
items.text:
Alternative dairy products are widely available in many countries. Grocery stores and cafes frequently offer “milks” made from soy, almond, oat, rice or other crops. That’s good news for people who don’t consume dairy, as well as for our planet, since the production of plant-based milk is more environmentally friendly than regular milk.
But relying on these plant-based alternatives—even partially—might carry health risks. In a study published in the September issue of the journal Lancet Planetary Health , researchers ran computer simulations based on United Kingdom nutrition data and found that swapping standard dairy for vegan versions can lead to deficiencies of four vital nutrients. However, that could be combated by mandating that nutrients be added to plant-based dairy alternatives, as well as bread, making them fortified foods .
Vegan milks, cheeses, yogurts, ice creams and more are becoming increasingly popular as people turn to them for health or sustainability reasons. However, they often lack certain nutrients found in dairy.
To explore the potential public health implications, researchers pulled data from the U.K.’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey involving more than 3,500 people between the ages of 1.5 and 100 years old. They put that information into a computer model to simulate how swapping out regular milk, yogurt and cheese with commercially available plant-based versions affected intake of four micronutrients: iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12.
The results weren’t great. Even replacing a modest amount of dairy caused a decline in intake of all analyzed micronutrients. Iodine took the biggest hit. Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make certain hormones, and it’s also crucial for brain development. The micronutrient is especially important for infants, adolescents and pregnant people.
The survey data revealed that 54 percent of girls ages 14 to 18 weren’t eating enough iodine. Replacing just 35 percent of dairy with plant-based alternatives would cause the deficiency to jump to 65 percent. Similarly, 32 percent of women ages 19 to 49 were iodine deficient at baseline, and it would rise to 42 percent after the same dairy swap.
If dairy intake was completely replaced, 80 percent of teenage girls and 72 percent of teenage boys would be iodine deficient, according to the computer simulations.

Martha penned the note on September 29, 1760. Writing to Margaret Bolan Green, she provided an update on her four-year-old daughter “Patsy.”
“I have the pleasure to tell you my dear little girl is much better,” she wrote. “She has lost her fitts & fevours bout and seems to be getting well very fast.”
The Library of Congress purchased the letter for $47,500 in June during a Heritage Auctions sale, with funding from the James Madison Council’s Edwin L. Sniffer dogs are being trained in Germany to detect potentially destructive invasive plants—alien species that are one of the main causes of biodiversity loss worldwide.
Scientists from Leipzig evaluated whether volunteer handlers and their dogs could be trained as effective detectives, and found the teams could locate invasive species in the wild with 75% accuracy.
Other methods to combat invasive species have been costly and time-consuming, and the lack of effective early-detection methods has limited ecologists’ ability to control further colonization by invasive species.
Dr. Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth and her colleagues at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) tested the feasibility of a volunteer dog-handler training program, so citizen scientists could join the fight.
31 dogs and their owners were trained between 2021 and 2023 using three highly problematic invasive plant species: Himalayan balsam, common ragweed, and those in the knotweed family, such as Japanese knotweed ( Fallopia spp. complex, Impatiens glandulifera, and Ambrosia artemisiifolia ).
The training culminated with a field test of the dogs’ ability to locate target species in the wild. Of the 12 teams that completed the field test, 11 teams passed, with an average detection success rate of 75%.
From the feasibility study, published in the journal PLOS One, the research team developed a set of recommendations to improve effectiveness of future, similar projects to improve volunteer selection and coordination, dog training, and initial deployments.
“Our study shows that trained volunteer dog-handler teams have real potential to support the early detection of invasive plants,” said Dr. Grimm-Seyfarth , in a media release.
“What we find particularly exciting is the opportunity to turn something people already love doing—spending time outdoors with their dogs—into a meaningful contribution to biodiversity conservation.”
“By combining dogs’ remarkable sense of smell with the enthusiasm of citizen scientists, we could expand monitoring efforts.
“With the right training, everyday walks could become an additional resource for detecting invasive plants early.”
Reliable monitoring requires more than a good nose, though. Training and continued guidance from both dog-training and ecological experts are needed to help volunteer teams succeed in real deployments.

A painting by Wassily Kandinsky , looted during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, has sold for £31.56 million (approximately $42 million) at Christie’s London. Completed in 1907, Das bunte Leben (The Colorful Life) was returned to the descendants of its original Jewish owners in 2023. Its October 14, 2026 auction result far exceeded the presale estimate of £18 million to £25 million.
Measuring approximately 5 by 4 feet, Das bunte Leben is an important early work by the Russian-born artist. It depicts a group of figures in a colorful, imagined landscape inspired by Russian folklore. The painting also reflects Kandinsky’s growing interest in expressive color and simplified forms, which would later inform his experiments with abstraction.
Dutch Jewish collectors Emanuel and Hedwig Lewenstein acquired the painting in 1927 and later loaned it to the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam. Following the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, the work appeared at auction in October 1940 without the family’s authorization. The Lewensteins received no proceeds. It subsequently passed through several private collections before German bank Bayerische Landesbank acquired it in 1972. The painting later entered a long-term loan to Munich’s Lenbachhaus museum.
The Lewenstein descendants spent decades pursuing the painting’s restitution. In 2023, a German advisory commission on Nazi-looted art determined that Nazi persecution had forced the family to lose the work. The commission recommended its return, and the painting was subsequently restituted to the heirs, ending decades of contested ownership.
More than a century after its creation, Das bunte Leben has returned to the art market with its provenance restored. Its $42 million sale marks a new chapter for the Kandinsky painting, following its long-awaited return to the family from whom it was taken.

Though a front yard covered in skeletons might serve to remind someone of their mortality, Wyche marveled at the creativity with which the homeowner arranged his decorations.
Some were raising the flag at Iwo Jima, while another was giving its dog a bone. There was a bony beekeeper who stood behind a cowboy riding an osseous equine, not far from where two boneheaded tourists were taking a selfie.
Yet despite this macabre menagerie, the scariest thing to Mr. Bill Pyle was what tended to show up in his Oxford, Ohio mailbox in those weeks leading up to Halloween—accusations of devil worship, promises of his expedient arrival in hell, and other such condemnations.
This carried on year after year, until one fateful day when Pyle opened a letter that he said stopped him “dead in his tracks.”
“I have been driving past your house daily for the past 19 days on my way to radiation treatments. A highlight of my journey has been checking to see who else has joined the bone family & what they are up to,” Wyche wrote in a heartfelt, handwritten correspondence.
“Thankfully, Wed. Sept 11th is my final radiation treatment, though I may need to continue to drive by once in a while to see what’s new. Thanks for the diversion.”
“Tears came to my eyes,” Pyle told CBS News’ ‘On the Road’ with Steve Hartman, remembering when he read it the first time. “[It]really touched my heart.”
Seeing the date of her final treatment, Pyle decided to roll the bones on a big surprise for this special admirer.
When Wyche drove past the ‘Bone Family’ that Wednesday morning, she looked to the right and saw a whole skeleton crew cheering her on with signs that celebrated this final milestone.
“It was very touching to think that somebody would go to that effort for a stranger,” she said.
Thanks to the story of Wyche’s brush with death at Pyle’s house, for every one person that has a bone to pick with him, there are 30—from as far away as Australia—sending messages of appreciation that encourage him to keep going with his skeletons.

items.text:
For generations, human cannibalism in prehistoric Europe was viewed as a desperate response to starvation. Now, a forensic re-examination of three prehistoric cave sites in southern Spain reveals that people ate human remains as a ritual for millennia, including after violent clashes or as a standard funeral rite.
Researchers analyzed 967 skeletal fragments representing at least 60 individuals recovered from the caves of Malalmuerzo , Carigüela and Majolicas in the province of Granada . Using high-resolution microscopy, machine learning and radiocarbon dating, the team discovered that these grisly feasts were not confined to a single crisis, such as war or starvation. Instead, they unfolded in “context-dependent episodes” between roughly 5300 B.C.E. and 3760 B.C.E., according to a recent study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science .
The bone assemblages were first excavated in the 1970s under the direction of Miguel C. Botella , a forensic anthropologist at the University of Granada. Fifty years later, Botella joined a multi-disciplinary team to subject the historical collection to modern forensic analysis.
“Returning to these materials with new tools has allowed us to address questions that were impossible to answer at the time,” lead author Palmira Saladié , an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution, explains in a statement .
By scrutinizing butchery traces, impact fractures and tooth marks under the microscope, the researchers distinguished between injuries inflicted on fresh bone around the time of death and natural degradation that took place years later. The skeletons bore unmistakable hallmarks of systematic butchery: defleshing cut marks, bones split open to harvest marrow, crushed crania to extract brain tissue and bones rendered translucent from boiling.

A ban on industrial scallop dredging has been “the most amazing thing to happen” to the residents, both man and marine, of the Summer Isles.
In place for 10 years, the ban has protected this extraordinary kind of magenta-colored seaweed called maerl, which forms hard, chalky nodules like coral on the seabed, and has allowed for whales, dolphins, porpoises, and key fish stocks to thrive.
Scallop dredging around the Summer Isles had damaged this incredible marine seascape for decades until a coalition of citizen scientists and activists got the activity banned inside a 150,000-acre protected area off the northwest coast of Scotland that contains all the area’s maerl beds, including 2 that are over a mile long which have been growing in the same place for 9,000 years.
Maerl builds up overtime into beds and carpets that interlock, creating magnificent marine habitat for fish species to breed.
Looking somewhat like the pieces from a game of knucklebones, the free movement of water between each nodule provides for excellent circulation which the foundational species of the marine food web need. They in turn provide for the species above and beyond them, all the way up to dolphins and humans.
The protections have been the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles,” one local activist and artist named Diyanna Ross told the Guardian. “It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.”
The Blue Hope Alliance, of which Ross is a part, also includes an association of Scottish “creel” fishermen, a smaller, more sustainable method of harvesting seafood that doesn’t deplete underlying stocks.
Decades of dredging had severely depleted scallop numbers, requiring industrial fishing operations to damage more and more seabed in search of the bivalves.
The 10-year-old campaign to ban scallop dredging, the Guardian reports , was as much about allowing these creel fishermen to continue to harvest scallops as it was about allowing the scallop to recover.

“After I pulled him out, I heard more screaming and realized there was another man lying at the bottom of the deep end, which was his son he was trying to save. Once I pulled the son out of the pool, I realized he was unconscious.”
The California Polytechnic State University Marine Academy cadet immediately began CPR on the son. After expelling water from his lungs, he was again breathing on his own.

items.title: The Handwritten Final Draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' Speech Was Considered Lost. It Turned Out to Be Sitting in a Desk Drawer for Decades
items.desc: Across seven yellow notepad pages, King is seen wrestling with word choice and revising his remarks the night before the March on Washington. The manuscript will head to auction in January and is expected to pull in more than $10 million
items.text:
It was late on August 27, 1963, and Martin Luther King Jr. was huddled with a group of his closest advisors in the lobby of the Willard Hotel in Washington, D.C.
They were drafting King’s closing remarks for the March on Washington , officially the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, which was set to start in just 12 hours. The group went back and forth on the message: Should it be ideological or Biblical? Directed towards the students marching or the nation at large?
As the night wore on, King eventually bowed out. “Okay brothers,” Clarence B. Jones , an activist and speechwriter for King, recalled him saying. “Thank you so much everybody for your suggestions and input … I am now going upstairs to my room to counsel with my Lord.”
Alone in his suite, King stayed up until 4 a.m., writing and revising his remarks on a yellow notepad, scratching out swaths of text in blue ink. He then sent these marked-up pages to be typed, forming the basis of his canonical “I Have a Dream” speech , delivered to more than 250,000 demonstrators gathered by the Lincoln Memorial .
Scholars have long assumed that the original, handwritten final draft had been discarded amid the day’s chaos. But six decades later, the manuscript has resurfaced from a drawer of one of King’s former aides. The seven yellow pages are set to be auctioned at Christie’s in January, where the draft is expected to sell for more than $10 million.
“When I first saw these pages and realized what they were, I was astounded,” Christie’s manuscripts specialist Peter Klarnet says in a statement . “This is a treasure of American history … Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr. King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time.”
Civil rights leader and philanthropist Xernona Clayton found the pages in the late 1990s. They were tucked in an envelope labeled “speech,” nestled among other papers in a desk drawer belonging to her late husband, Edward , one of King’s aides and speechwriters.
Clayton knew it was an important document related to the “I Have a Dream” speech but not that it was the final manuscript. She tucked it back in the desk drawer, not wanting to disrespect King’s memory by selling or displaying his memorabilia.
But in recent years, she changed her mind. “Now that I’m older, I’m wiser,” Clayton, now 96, tells the New York Times ’ Jennifer Schuessler. “It just seems like something that important ought to be shared.”

items.text:
Swans and ducks have enjoyed the wetland reserve at Slimbridge for 80 years
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.
Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).
Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.
Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."
Sir Peter Scott feeds migrating swans and geese at Slimbridge in 1947, with Desmond Hawkins, BBC features producer from Bristol
WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.
Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change.
So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change?

In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes.
Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl.
He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them.
Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl.

As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature.

Benefits of baxdrostat are unexpectedly found to remain up to two years after patients stop taking it
Millions of people with high blood pressure stand to benefit from a new drug that has stunned doctors by reversing a common cause of the condition for years after patients stopped taking the medication.
Patients who took the drug, called baxdrostat, saw their blood pressure improve during a six- to 12-month course of the daily pills, but unexpectedly the benefits remained up to two years later, with some patients no longer on any hypertension drugs and potentially cured of the condition.
“It’s very exciting to see,” said Prof Morris Brown, a hypertension specialist at Queen Mary University of London, who led the study. “Just under a quarter of the patients came off all treatment and had completely normal blood pressure.”
More than a billion people worldwide have high blood pressure, or hypertension, including more than 12 million in the UK. In 5 to 10% of cases, the condition is caused by small nodules or benign tumours on the adrenal glands that cause them to overproduce a hormone called aldosterone. The excess hormone raises blood pressure by signalling the kidneys to retain salt.
The standard treatment for what is called primary aldosteronism is to surgically remove the affected adrenal gland, but other factors can contribute to the patient’s hypertension, meaning surgery is not always a complete cure.
Baxdrostat is known as an aldosterone synthase inhibitor (ASI) which suppresses the blood pressure-raising hormone. The drug was approved in the US earlier this year for patients with hypertension that is not controlled by existing drugs. It is being assessed by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice), which could make the drug available through the NHS next year.
The potentially curative effect of baxdrostat came to light in a small study that followed 14 patients whose hypertension improved dramatically during a three-month trial of the drug. They continued taking the daily pills for six to 12 months and then stopped. When doctors checked the patients up to two years later, their blood pressure was still lower. Details are published in the New England Journal of Medicine .

items.desc: There's so much about the world we don't know, and sometimes, one photo is all it takes to teach us something new! So, we've gathered some fascinating pictures that might leave you a little wiser. Keep scrolling to see how many you already knew about!
items.text:
A good idea can come to anyone, anywhere. Sometimes, it happens while working on a big project. Other times, it strikes in the middle of an ordinary day, when something doesn't work the way it should. Before you know it, a small idea can become something millions of people use.
Since today's post is all about interesting things, we thought we'd share some equally interesting stories behind a few inventions. Some came from unexpected situations, while others were created simply to make life a little easier. And the people behind them have quite a story to tell!
Consider the pull-tab can, for example. In 1959, engineer Ermal “Ernie” Fraze went on a picnic and realized he forgot a can opener. He ended up using a car bumper to open his drink.
The experience got him thinking about how to make opening cans easier. A few years later, he invented the pull-tab can , letting customers open their drinks without a separate tool. What started as a minor annoyance eventually transformed how millions of people enjoyed their drinks.
And Fraze wasn't the only inventor to be inspired by a common problem. In the 1930s, Joseph Friedman watched his daughter Judith struggle to swallow a milkshake at his brother’s soda shop.
The straight straw was beyond her reach. So he put a screw into a paper straw and wrapped dental floss around it. Once he removed the screw, the straw could bend. He patented the flexible straw in 1937. What began as a parent helping his daughter has now become an idea utilized in homes, restaurants and hospitals around the world.
Both inventions solved simple problems that many people had probably faced. But sometimes, the idea is merely the beginning of the story. Consider engineer Robert Kearns.
He was driving in mild rain and realized what a pain windscreen wipers can be. But back then they generally worked at fixed speeds, even if the rain wasn't steady. Kearns pondered why wipers couldn't stop between sweeps, as our eyes blink. He ultimately developed a technique that did just that and patented it.

But things didn’t go exactly as they had intended. Car makers later used similar technology, leading Kearns to spend years fighting for recognition and compensation.
He eventually won legal disputes with Ford and Chrysler. His story shows that inventing something valuable doesn’t always lead to a smooth path to success. Sometimes the hardest part of a concept is getting it down on paper.

items.desc: A new study reveals the step-by-step process some octopuses use to cram themselves into tight openings. The findings could inspire new designs for soft robots used during search-and-rescue missions
items.text:
Octopuses are talented escape artists, capable of squeezing their bodies through seemingly impenetrable gaps to avoid danger, find hidden prey or break out of captivity . Scientists have long wondered how these eight-limbed creatures manage such impressive feats of flexibility. Now, they say they have some answers.
A study published November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology describes the step-by-step processes some octopuses use to cram themselves into tight spaces. In addition to expanding our understanding of these crafty cephalopods, the findings could help engineers improve the design of soft robots that need to fit into small spaces, such as those used during search-and-rescue missions.
“You always just think as a biologist that this is a minor question: How to squeeze your body into a crevice, through a hole or into a cave,” study co-author Michael Kuba , a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, tells IFLScience ’s Rachael Funnell. “But working with soft robotic engineers, you realize that there is so much more to how they manage to do this. They have several steps of the movement, and they have specific postures and body parts they use to move through a hole.”
In the study, Kuba and colleagues conducted laboratory experiments involving three subadult common octopuses ( Octopus vulgaris ) and four juvenile Mayan octopuses ( O. maya ). The team started by measuring the distance between each animal’s eyes to determine the size of the semi-rigid cartilage casing surrounding their brains. Then, they adjusted a clear, acrylic tank partition to create a single, central hole that was either smaller or larger than the measurements, which ranged from about 0.4 to 1.4 inches. One at a time, they placed the octopuses in the tank, then watched and filmed what happened next.
“We know that they can squeeze through all these spaces, but nobody’s actually looked at how they do this,” study co-author Tamar Gutnick , a biologist at the Haus des Meeres-Aqua Terra Zoo in Austria, tells NPR ’s Ari Daniel. “So, what we did was take octopuses and systematically make them go through different-sized holes.”
Octopus bodies are mostly soft and pliable. These creatures have only two stiffer body parts: a cartilaginous shell that protects their brains and a beak —made of a hard material called chitin—that they use to eat.

From the brink of extinction to roaming across 6,500 square miles, populations of Cantabrian brown bears have doubled in Spain over the last 20 years to 370.
Numbering as few as 140 by estimates in the early 21st century, they’re another example of Spain’s ongoing success in protecting several of the country’s endemic species.
Taking its name from the far northern Spanish region whose mountains stand as the bear’s last redoubt, Cantabrian brown bears can actually be found across the regions of Asturians, Leon, Galicia, and Palencia, in addition to Cantabria.
By restricting the movement of animals, the Iberian Peninsula’s northern mountain ranges have led to high rates of endemism in Spain and Portugal among animals such as the wolf, lynx, and bear.
Direct human persecution and the conversion of wilderness to agricultural land gradually impacted the brown bear’s numbers until they could only be found in Cantabria. Yet they clung to existence in the mountains until sufficient protections were put in place for them to gain a second wind.
A study published in 2023 bears witness to the successful survival and spread by Spain’s bears. Published in the journal Conservation Science and Practice, it found that the government’s continual protection measures and establishment of new protected areas, coupled with rural depopulation, allowed the bears to substantially recover.
Using all data available to them, the authors measured the changes in population numbers across 3 periods: from 1982 to 1992, from 1993 to 2002, and from 2003 to 2012.
While a 25% reduction in the numbers of bears was observed between the first 2 periods, this was followed by a 70% increase by the end of the 3rd period. That final period also saw their breeding ranges expand by 30%, such that Cantabria’s 2 breeding populations now overlap, having been separated for decades by an 18-24 mile series of gorges with a highway running through them.
The first 2 periods coincided with the creation of Somiedo Natural Park and Redes National Park respectively, which increased the amount of protected areas centered on the last remaining populations of brown bears 688 square kilometers. Fines for unauthorized killing of bears reached some $350,000.
Additional growth in the geographical range of 77% was observed by the authors between 2013 and 2022 in exactly the proportion and areas they predicted.
